title: Animal Behavior / Ethology
short: What animals do, how behavior develops and changes, and why behavioral patterns occur.
bigPicture: Animal behavior examines actions, communication, learning, social relationships, decision-making, and responses to the environment. It can be studied in wild, companion, farm, laboratory, shelter, or zoo animals.

focus.title: Social and reproductive behavior
focus.description: Social and reproductive behavior includes bonding, dominance, cooperation, conflict, courtship, mate choice, parental care, and group organization. Researchers examine both immediate causes and evolutionary consequences.

focus.title: Communication and sensory behavior
focus.description: Animals communicate through sound, scent, posture, touch, vibration, color, and electrical or chemical signals. Sensory research asks what animals can detect and how that information guides action.

focus.title: Learning and behavioral development
focus.description: Learning changes behavior through experience; development examines how behavior emerges across an animal’s life. Studies may separate inherited tendencies, early experience, social exposure, training, and current conditions.

focus.title: Foraging, movement, and environmental responses
focus.description: Foraging and movement research examines how animals locate resources, evaluate risk, navigate, choose habitats, and adjust to weather, predators, competitors, people, or changes in their environment.

questions: Why does an animal choose one social partner, food source, or habitat over another?
How do animals communicate and interpret signals?
How do social and environmental conditions affect behavior?
responsibilities: Define behaviors clearly and develop an observation or coding system.
Observe animals directly or from video and record behavior systematically.
Design experiments or compare behavior across individuals, groups, species, or conditions.
Analyze behavioral data and explain conclusions, uncertainty, and practical implications.
knowledgeSkills: Ethology, evolution, ecology, and natural history

variations.label: Purpose
variations.description: Behavior research may build basic knowledge or support welfare, training, conservation, or management decisions.

variations.label: Setting
variations.description: The work can occur in natural habitats, zoos, farms, shelters, homes, laboratories, or through archived video and datasets.

variations.label: Animal contact
variations.description: Systematic observation may involve little handling; applied training and husbandry may involve frequent direct contact.

variations.label: Career structure
variations.description: Technician and applied roles can be B.S.-accessible, while independent research positions usually require graduate training.

realities: Behavioral research can involve long periods of observation, coding, data cleaning, and writing.
Interesting animal behavior does not necessarily mean frequent animal handling.
Applied roles often require substantial hands-on experience in addition to academic knowledge.
Behavioral explanations must separate evidence from assumptions about intention or emotion.
careers: Animal behaviorist / applied animal behavior scientist
